title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill
edition_analyzed: Standard edition, typically the original unabridged text
target_audience: Students and scholars of philosophy and political science
General readers exploring concepts of freedom and individuality
core_themes: The importance of individual liberty and autonomy
The limits of authority and societal control
The harm principle—where society may rightfully limit individual conduct
Diversity of opinions as a source of societal progress
primary_purpose: To argue for the protection and value of individual freedoms against the encroachment of society and government, and to establish guiding principles for when power can justifiably be exercised over individuals.

structure_format.organization: Divided into five chapters, each developing a central argument or aspect of liberty
features: Occasional references to other thinkers and political contexts

key_concepts_lessons: Individual liberty is valuable both for personal development and the greater good of society.
Society may only restrict individual freedom to prevent harm to others—known as the harm principle.
Freedom of expression and dissent are essential for the discovery of truth and social advancement.
Conformity and ‘tyranny of the majority’ are dangers to personal liberty.
Tolerating diverse lifestyles and opinions enriches society.
notable_features: Influential in debates on civil rights, free speech, and law
Addresses both legal and social constraints on liberty
cultural_historical_context: Published during the Victorian era in Britain, ‘On Liberty’ responded to expanding democratic participation and rising social conformity. Mill’s work engaged with Enlightenment ideals and ongoing debates about the role of government, the rights of the individual, and limits of majority rule in a rapidly changing society.
reception_impact: Highly influential in shaping modern liberal thought and doctrines of civil liberties
Frequently cited in legal, political, and academic debates regarding freedom and rights
Praised for its clarity and forceful defense of individual autonomy
Criticized by some for insufficient emphasis on social obligations and community
Continues to inform constitutional law, human rights debates, and liberal political philosophy
comparable_titles: Two Treatises of Government by John Locke
The Social Contract by Jean-Jacques Rousseau
Democracy in America by Alexis de Tocqueville
